messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Ramesh, an eighty-year-old widower, carried the weight of a moment from his long career in the Coast Guard. Decades ago, during a fierce storm off the New England coast, his cutter was responding to a distress call from a small fishing vessel. In the chaos of the rescue, as a fisherman was being brought aboard, a sudden, violent swell caused a piece of heavy equipment to swing wildly. Ramesh, in his haste to secure it, misjudged the force, and the davit arm struck the fisherman, causing a severe head injury. The man survived but was permanently disabled, a fact that etched itself into Ramesh’s soul.

In the immediate aftermath, Ramesh found his memories of the incident were a jumble. When he tried to deliberately remember what happened, he found it difficult to access the memory; it was like trying to grasp smoke. Instead, his memories of the event came in disconnected pieces that did not fit together – a flash of the man’s face, the cold spray of the ocean, the metallic clang, but never a coherent sequence. Yet, sometimes, without warning, the memory would return, feeling completely real across all his senses at once: the smell of the salty air, the roar of the wind, the sickening thud, and the desperate shouts. To cope, Ramesh had developed a habit of trying to push these thoughts out of his mind. He would tell himself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, a desperate attempt at magical thinking. He would force himself to think only positive thoughts, but the relief was always fleeting.

Over the years, a profound sense of self-blame had taken root. He had come to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he was—flawed, prone to making catastrophic mistakes. This belief fueled a constant need to be on guard all the time, as if his inherent defectiveness might manifest again at any moment.

Now, in his retirement, his world had grown small. He lived in a quiet coastal town, but being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, particularly near the sea or in open, windswept areas, would bring a wave of unease and dread. He avoided the scenic coastal paths he and his late wife used to enjoy, opting instead for the enclosed safety of his small home. The piercing wail of sirens, whether from an ambulance or a police car, would instantly transport him back to the frantic urgency of that day, his heart pounding with the echoes of old panic. Even talking about the future became a source of anxiety. When his grandchildren spoke of their plans, he would grow quiet, certain that his presence might somehow taint their prospects, or that his own defective nature would inevitably lead to more harm.

He found himself avoiding going to unfamiliar places because he felt he could not assess the danger, a lingering fear that he would once again fail to protect himself or others. When he did venture out, he would always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt, often with his back to a wall, facing the exit. In a strange, almost contradictory way, he also found himself taking too many risks or doing things that could cause him harm, perhaps a subconscious form of self-punishment or a desperate attempt to feel something other than the crushing weight of his past. The once vibrant social life he shared with his wife had dwindled. He declined invitations to community events, particularly those held outdoors or in new venues, leaving him increasingly isolated.

The recent passing of his wife had intensified his solitude, leaving him with more time for his thoughts to circle. He had finally sought help, not out of hope for a cure, but out of a quiet desperation. He was tired of the constant vigilance, tired of the fragmented memories, and most of all, he was afraid of dying with this heavy burden still weighing on his soul, believing himself to be fundamentally defective to the very end.
